title: Computer history
description: Sourced milestones for the interactive timeline at /science/tech/computer-history/.

events.title: Counting boards and the abacus
events.summary: Counting boards were used around the ancient Mediterranean to reckon with counters. The framed bead abacus familiar from later trade is a related instrument, not a single dated invention.
events.note: No single invention year is known. This entry uses the mid-first millennium BCE as a reading point for counting boards, not a claim about one workshop.

events.title: Antikythera mechanism
events.summary: A geared Greek device recovered from a shipwreck computed astronomical cycles. It is the oldest known machine of that complexity.
events.note: Britannica dates manufacture to around 100 BCE. Other research places the device earlier in the second century BCE. It predates a wreck dated to roughly 70–60 BCE.

events.title: Napier's bones
events.summary: John Napier described a set of numbered rods that turn multiplication and division into addition along a column. They are a calculating aid, not a machine with moving gears.

events.title: The slide rule
events.summary: William Oughtred arranged logarithmic scales so they could slide against each other. For three centuries the slide rule was the everyday tool of engineers who needed products, quotients, and roots.

events.title: Schickard's calculating clock
events.summary: Wilhelm Schickard described a calculating clock in letters to Kepler. It combined Napier-style rods with a geared adder.
events.note: The original machine does not survive. Later reconstructions rely on the letters and sketches, so parts of the 1623 design remain disputed.

events.title: Pascal's adding machine
events.summary: Blaise Pascal built a geared adder, the Pascaline, to help with his father's tax arithmetic. It handled addition and subtraction through dials and carry wheels.

events.title: Leibniz's stepped reckoner
events.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz demonstrated a calculator meant to multiply as well as add, using a stepped drum. A reliable four-function machine still lay ahead.

events.title: Jacquard loom
events.summary: Joseph-Marie Jacquard patented a loom head that read punched cards to lift warp threads for a pattern. The same card idea later fed numbers and instructions into calculating engines.

sources.title: Science and Industry Museum — Jacquard loom

events.title: Babbage's Difference Engine
events.summary: Charles Babbage proposed a machine that would compute and print polynomial tables by the method of finite differences. A complete engine was not finished in his lifetime.

events.title: Babbage's Analytical Engine
events.summary: Babbage designed a general machine with a store, a mill, and control from punched cards borrowed from the Jacquard loom. It was never completed, but the plan separates memory from arithmetic in a way later computers repeat.

events.title: Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine
events.summary: Ada Lovelace published an annotated translation of Menabrea's account of the Analytical Engine. Her notes include a worked procedure for Bernoulli numbers and argue that the engine could operate on symbols other than quantities.

sources.title: Science and Industry Museum — Jacquard loom

events.title: Boole's laws of thought
events.summary: George Boole published a system in which logical claims could be written and combined like algebra. That calculus later mapped onto relay and transistor circuits.

events.title: Hollerith's census tabulator
events.summary: Herman Hollerith's punched-card machines tallied the 1890 United States census. Electric sensing of cards turned counting into a business, and the company that grew from the work became IBM.

events.title: Turing's computable numbers
events.summary: Alan Turing defined a theoretical machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape. The paper draws a precise line around what such a machine can compute.

sources.title: London Mathematical Society — On Computable Numbers

events.title: Stibitz's Model K adder
events.summary: George Stibitz built a relay adder on a kitchen table to show that Boolean logic could drive telephone relays. The demonstration led Bell Labs toward larger relay calculators.

events.title: Shannon's relay logic
events.summary: Claude Shannon showed that switching circuits could be designed with Boolean algebra. The thesis gave engineers a language for relays and, later, electronic logic.

events.title: Zuse's Z1
events.summary: Konrad Zuse completed a mechanical binary calculator in Berlin, programmed from punched tape. It was unreliable, and it led directly to his relay machines.

sources.title: Deutsches Patent- und Markenamt — Konrad Zuse

events.title: Remote use of the Complex Number Calculator
events.summary: Bell Labs finished Stibitz's Complex Number Calculator, and he demonstrated it from Dartmouth over a teletype line to New York. The session is an early case of computing at a distance.

events.title: The Turing-Welchman Bombe
events.summary: The British Bombe, developed from a Polish design, searched for Enigma rotor settings. Allied codebreaking used the machines in large numbers during the war.

events.title: Zuse demonstrates the Z3
events.summary: Konrad Zuse presented the Z3 in Berlin, a relay machine that used binary floating-point arithmetic and a punched-tape program. The original was destroyed in a wartime air raid. A later reconstruction is at the Deutsches Museum.

events.title: Atanasoff-Berry Computer
events.summary: John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built an electronic special-purpose machine at Iowa State for systems of linear equations. A 1973 court ruling later treated their work as prior art against the ENIAC patent.

events.title: Colossus at Bletchley Park
events.summary: Tommy Flowers' Colossus, a vacuum-tube machine, was delivered to Bletchley Park to attack the Lorenz cipher. Its existence stayed secret until the 1970s.

sources.title: The National Museum of Computing — Colossus

events.note: The National Museum of Computing dates delivery to late December 1943 or January 1944, with the machine working in early February 1944. A National Archives memo records arrival on 18 January 1944.

events.title: Harvard Mark I
events.summary: IBM built Howard Aiken's Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, a room-sized relay machine, for Harvard. It produced mathematical tables and was soon overtaken by electronic stored-program computers.

events.title: The Curta calculator
events.summary: Curt Herzstark refined a pocket-sized stepped-drum calculator while imprisoned at Buchenwald, and production began after the war. The Curta remained a favored mechanical calculator into the electronic era.
events.note: Herzstark's design work dates to his imprisonment from 1943. Commercial Curtas were built after the war. This entry marks the start of production rather than the camp sketches.

events.title: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
events.summary: John von Neumann circulated a draft describing a stored-program computer, with instructions and data kept in the same electronic memory. The report spread the architecture that many postwar projects copied.

events.title: ENIAC is dedicated
events.summary: The US Army and the University of Pennsylvania unveiled ENIAC, a vacuum-tube machine programmed with plugs and switches. The Computer History Museum describes it as occupying more than 1,000 square feet and using about 18,000 tubes.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — ENIAC in the New York Times
US Army Research Laboratory — ENIAC dates

events.title: Moore School lectures
events.summary: A summer course at the University of Pennsylvania walked visitors through electronic computing. Participants left to build stored-program machines, including Maurice Wilkes, who went on to EDSAC.

events.title: Point-contact transistor
events.summary: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working with William Shockley at Bell Labs, demonstrated a point-contact transistor. It replaced the vacuum tube's role as a switch in later computers, once manufacturing caught up.
events.note: The laboratory demonstration was in December 1947. Accounts differ on the day, often 16 or 23 December. Bell Labs announced the work publicly in 1948.

events.title: Manchester Baby runs a stored program
events.summary: Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn, and Geoff Tootill ran a 17-instruction program on the Small-Scale Experimental Machine. It was the first program executed from electronic memory on a digital computer.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — The stored program

events.title: EDSAC runs its first program
events.summary: Maurice Wilkes's team at Cambridge ran the first program on EDSAC, a vacuum-tube machine with mercury delay-line memory. It became a regular computing service for the university, with a library of subroutines on paper tape.

events.title: Ferranti Mark 1
events.summary: Ferranti delivered a Mark 1, grown from the Manchester machines, to Manchester University. It is often counted as the first commercially available general-purpose computer.
events.note: The Computer History Museum says the title of first commercial general-purpose computer "probably" belongs to the Ferranti Mark 1. Other machines were close behind.

events.title: UNIVAC I reaches the Census Bureau
events.summary: Remington Rand delivered the first UNIVAC I, designed by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, to the US Census Bureau. It was the electronic computer that first drew wide public attention in the United States.

events.title: LEO I, a computer for business
events.summary: J. Lyons and Company built LEO, modeled on EDSAC, to schedule bakery production and deliveries. It did useful commercial work in Britain ahead of most business installations elsewhere.

events.title: Whirlwind and magnetic-core memory
events.summary: MIT's Whirlwind, begun as a Navy flight simulator and finished as a digital computer, became the proving ground for Jay Forrester's magnetic-core memory. Core remained the usual fast memory into the 1970s.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Memory and storage

events.title: IBM 701
events.summary: IBM shipped the 701 electronic data processing machine to laboratories and government customers. It marked IBM's entry into large-scale electronic computing.

events.title: IBM 650
events.summary: The IBM 650 magnetic-drum calculator became IBM's first mass-produced computer. Universities used it widely, and a generation of students learned to program on it.

events.title: Turing's imitation game
events.summary: Alan Turing's paper in Mind proposed an imitation game as a way to talk about machine intelligence. The setup is now usually called the Turing test.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: TX-0, a transistor computer
events.summary: MIT Lincoln Laboratory built the TX-0, an early general-purpose computer constructed with transistors rather than tubes. It later hosted playful experiments in interactive programming.

events.title: IBM 305 RAMAC disk storage
events.summary: IBM announced the 305 RAMAC, the first commercial computer with a moving-head hard disk. Random access to a stack of disks changed how business files could be stored.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Memory and storage

events.title: FORTRAN
events.summary: An IBM team led by John Backus delivered FORTRAN, a scientific language whose statements read closer to algebra than to machine code. It became the usual language of technical computing and is still in use.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: LISP
events.summary: John McCarthy devised LISP at MIT, a language in which programs and data are both lists. That symmetry suited the symbolic work of early artificial intelligence.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: Kilby's integrated circuit
events.summary: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated a circuit with its parts formed in one piece of semiconductor. The integrated circuit is the reason later computers could shrink.

events.title: Dartmouth summer project on artificial intelligence
events.summary: A summer research project at Dartmouth College brought together early workers on machine reasoning and used the name artificial intelligence for the field. The 1955 proposal is usually treated as the founding document.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.note: The proposal is dated 1955. The conference itself was held in the summer of 1956.

events.title: COBOL
events.summary: A committee drawn from manufacturers and the US Department of Defense defined COBOL for business data. It aimed to be readable and to move, with a compiler, from one machine to another.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Noyce's planar integrated circuit
events.summary: Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a practical monolithic integrated circuit using the planar process. Kilby's 1958 demonstration and Noyce's manufacturable design are both claimed as the invention of the chip.

events.title: DEC PDP-1
events.summary: Digital Equipment Corporation introduced the PDP-1, a minicomputer with a cathode-ray display that one person could operate. At MIT it became the machine Spacewar! ran on.

events.title: Compatible Time-Sharing System
events.summary: Fernando Corbató's group at MIT demonstrated CTSS on a modified IBM 7090. Many people could share one machine from terminals, and the system included early messaging between users.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Spacewar!
events.summary: Steve Russell and other MIT students wrote Spacewar! on the PDP-1, a two-player game of ships maneuvering around a star. It is the set piece of early interactive computer graphics.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Graphics and games

events.title: Atlas and virtual memory
events.summary: Manchester, Ferranti, and Plessey brought the Atlas online. It was among the fastest machines of its day and introduced virtual memory, treating a drum as an extension of main store, under the Atlas Supervisor.

events.title: Sutherland's Sketchpad
events.summary: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad let a person draw on a screen with a light pen and have the computer enforce geometric constraints. It is a founding demonstration of interactive graphics.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: ASCII
events.summary: The American Standard Code for Information Interchange assigned numbers to letters, digits, and controls. A shared code meant machines could exchange text without a private alphabet.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: IBM System/360
events.summary: IBM announced the System/360 family. Models across a wide performance range could run the same software, and the bet shifted IBM's business from punched-card machines toward electronic systems.

events.title: BASIC at Dartmouth
events.summary: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz created BASIC so students who were not programmers could write programs on a time-sharing system. Later personal computers shipped with dialects of the language.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: CDC 6600
events.summary: Control Data introduced the 6600, designed under Seymour Cray. The Computer History Museum describes it as performing up to 3 million instructions per second, then the fastest computer available.

events.title: SABRE reservations
events.summary: American Airlines and IBM put the SABRE reservation system into operation on dual IBM 7090 mainframes. It grew from earlier air-defense work and became a model for online transaction systems.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: PDP-8
events.summary: DEC introduced the PDP-8, a small general-purpose computer that sold for a fraction of a mainframe. Thousands went to labs, factories, and businesses, and the minicomputer category stuck.

events.title: DENDRAL
events.summary: Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg, and Bruce Buchanan's DENDRAL inferred chemical structures from mass-spectrometer data. It is one of the first expert systems, encoding specialist rules in software.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: Multics begins
events.summary: MIT, Bell Labs, and General Electric started Multics, a multi-user operating system with shared files and strong protection between users. Bell Labs later withdrew. The ideas, and the name, fed Unix.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.note: 1965 marks the start of the joint project. Usable Multics systems followed later in the decade.

events.title: ELIZA
events.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA at MIT carried on a typed dialogue by pattern matching, most famously as a parody of a Rogerian therapist. People attributed more understanding to it than the program had.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: Simula 67
events.summary: Kristen Nygaard and Ole-Johan Dahl developed Simula for simulations, and with it the class and object ideas later languages inherited. Simula is the usual starting point for object-oriented programming.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Engelbart's oN-Line System demo
events.summary: Douglas Engelbart's group at SRI demonstrated the mouse, hypertext, windows, and collaborative editing in a single public session. The event is often called the mother of all demos.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web
Computer History Museum — Input and output

events.title: Unix
events.summary: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie began Unix at Bell Labs on a spare DEC minicomputer, after Multics. It kept time-sharing and a simple file model, and it became the ancestor of a large family of systems.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.note: The Computer History Museum places the start of Unix in 1969. The first widely circulated manuals and the C rewrite came in the early 1970s.

events.title: First ARPANET message
events.summary: A computer at UCLA sent the first message over the ARPANET to the Stanford Research Institute. The network was a four-node experiment in connecting different kinds of computers.

events.title: PDP-11
events.summary: DEC introduced the PDP-11, a 16-bit minicomputer whose clean instruction set and bus showed up in labs everywhere. Unix grew up on it.

events.title: Pascal
events.summary: Niklaus Wirth introduced Pascal, a teaching language with strict types and a structure meant to be read. It spread through universities and, later, early microcomputers.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: The 8-inch floppy disk
events.summary: IBM introduced an 8-inch flexible magnetic disk for loading microcode and moving data. Smaller floppies later became the portable medium of personal computers.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Memory and storage

events.title: Network email
events.summary: Ray Tomlinson at BBN sent mail between machines on the ARPANET, choosing the @ sign to separate the user from the host. Mail became the network's first everyday use.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Intel 4004
events.summary: Intel advertised the 4004, a 4-bit microprocessor designed with Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stan Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima for a Busicom calculator. It was the first general-purpose microprocessor sold as a component.

events.title: The C programming language
events.summary: Dennis Ritchie developed C at Bell Labs while Unix was being rewritten in a higher-level language. C stayed close to the machine and became the language of operating systems and tools.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages
Nokia Bell Labs — The C programming language

events.title: Pong
events.summary: Atari's Pong, a coin-operated table-tennis game, went into a Sunnyvale bar and then into production. It took video games out of the lab and into public rooms.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Graphics and games

events.note: Atari installed a prototype at Andy Capp's Tavern in November 1972. Production cabinets followed.

events.title: Smalltalk at Xerox PARC
events.summary: Alan Kay's group at Xerox PARC began Smalltalk, a language and environment built around objects, a graphical screen, and a mouse. The widely published Smalltalk-80 books came later.
events.note: Work on Smalltalk started in the early 1970s. The Smalltalk-80 release that left PARC is usually dated 1980, with the main books in the early 1980s.

events.title: Xerox Alto
events.summary: Xerox PARC built the Alto, a personal workstation with a bitmap display, windows, a mouse, and a local network. Apple's Lisa and Macintosh later carried many of its ideas to a market.

events.title: Ethernet memo
events.summary: Robert Metcalfe wrote a Xerox PARC memo describing a shared-cable local network he called the Ether network. Ethernet became the usual way to connect machines in an office.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Micral
events.summary: The French company R2E sold the Micral, an early commercial personal computer built on the Intel 8008. It was aimed at control jobs that did not need a minicomputer.

events.title: Community Memory
events.summary: Community Memory placed public terminals in Berkeley so people could post and search notices on a shared computer. It was an early experiment in a computerized bulletin board for a neighborhood.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Cerf and Kahn's internetworking paper
events.summary: Vint Cerf and Robert Kahn published a design for connecting different packet networks. The work became TCP/IP, the common language of the Internet.

sources.title: IEEE — A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication

events.title: Intel 8080
events.summary: Intel introduced the 8080, an 8-bit microprocessor that could address far more memory than the 8008 and needed fewer support chips. It powered the Altair and the CP/M generation.

events.title: CP/M
events.summary: Gary Kildall developed CP/M, a disk operating system for Intel 8080 machines. It let software move among microcomputers that shared the operating system rather than one brand of hardware.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Altair 8800
events.summary: Popular Electronics put the MITS Altair 8800 on its January cover. The kit, built around an Intel 8080, sold in the thousands and gave hobbyists a computer of their own.

events.title: Altair BASIC
events.summary: Bill Gates and Paul Allen licensed a BASIC interpreter to MITS as the language for the Altair. It was the first product of the partnership that became Microsoft.

events.title: MOS Technology 6502
events.summary: Chuck Peddle's team introduced the 6502 at a low price next to Intel and Motorola parts. The Apple II, the Commodore PET, and later the Nintendo Entertainment System used it or a close relative.

events.title: Cray-1
events.summary: Seymour Cray's Cray-1 reached customers as the fastest machine of its day. Its C-shaped cabinet shortened wires, and a Freon system cooled a dense pack of circuits.

events.title: Zilog Z80
events.summary: Zilog, founded by Federico Faggin, introduced the Z80, an 8080-compatible microprocessor with more registers and a single 5-volt supply. It ran CP/M machines, the TRS-80, and a long tail of embedded gear.
events.note: The Computer History Museum groups the 8080 and the Z80 in its 1976 computers entry. The 8080 itself dates to 1974. This entry is the Z80 introduction in 1976.

events.title: Apple-1
events.summary: Steve Wozniak designed the Apple-1 as a single-board computer, and Steve Jobs sold it. About two hundred boards were made before the Apple II.

events.title: Apple II
events.summary: Apple sold the Apple II as a finished computer with a keyboard, color graphics, and a case. It stayed in production for many years and put personal computers into schools.

events.title: TRS-80
events.summary: Tandy Radio Shack introduced the TRS-80, a Z80 desktop with a monitor, BASIC, and cassette storage, sold in its own stores. It found a large home and school audience.

events.title: Commodore PET
events.summary: Commodore introduced the PET, a complete computer with a MOS 6502, a built-in cassette, and a chiclet keyboard. It was one of the three home machines of 1977, with the Apple II and the TRS-80.

events.title: VAX-11/780
events.summary: DEC introduced the VAX, a 32-bit successor to the PDP-11 with a large virtual address space. VAX and VMS became a standard scientific and commercial minicomputer platform.

events.title: CBBS, the first public BBS
events.summary: Ward Christensen and Randy Suess opened the Computerized Bulletin Board System in Chicago so hobbyists with modems could leave and read messages. Dial-up boards spread from that pattern.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Intel 8086
events.summary: Intel introduced the 8086, a 16-bit microprocessor whose instruction set became the x86 line. The IBM PC used the related 8088, with an 8-bit external bus.

events.title: VisiCalc
events.summary: Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston's VisiCalc turned the Apple II into a business tool by making a visible ledger that recalculated. The spreadsheet gave people a reason to buy a personal computer.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Motorola 68000
events.summary: Motorola introduced the 68000, a 16/32-bit microprocessor with a large flat address space. It powered workstations and home computers including the Macintosh, the Amiga, and the Atari ST.

events.title: Atari 400 and 800
events.summary: Atari released the 400 and 800, home computers with strong graphics and sound next to its game console. They became tools for games, art, and the demoscene.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer
events.summary: IBM announced the Model 5150, a personal computer built on an Intel 8088 and Microsoft's DOS. Clones of its open design created the PC industry.

events.title: MS-DOS
events.summary: Microsoft supplied the disk operating system for the IBM PC, bought in from the 86-DOS work of Tim Paterson and adapted as PC-DOS and MS-DOS. It became the software platform of PC clones.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Osborne 1
events.summary: The Osborne 1 was the first portable computer sold in volume, a heavy case with a small screen, two floppy drives, and a bundle of software. It defined the luggable, if not the laptop.

events.title: Commodore 64
events.summary: Commodore introduced the 64, a home computer with 64 kilobytes of RAM and capable graphics and sound. The Computer History Museum records it as the best-selling single computer model, with more than 22 million units.

events.title: Minitel opens to the public
events.summary: France Telecom's Minitel put a small terminal in homes and businesses for a national videotex service, including directories and message boards. It was a mass online system years before the Web.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Sun Microsystems
events.summary: Andy Bechtolsheim, Vinod Khosla, Scott McNealy, and Bill Joy founded Sun around a Unix workstation with networking and a high-resolution display. The model defined engineering workstations for a decade.

events.title: Compact disc
events.summary: Sony and Philips brought the compact disc to market as a digital audio disc read by a laser. CD-ROM later used the same physical disc as computer storage.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Memory and storage

events.title: ARPANET switches to TCP/IP
events.summary: On 1 January 1983 the ARPANET required TCP/IP and dropped its older host protocol. DARPA treats that cutover as the point at which the ARPANET had become an internet of networks.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: GNU Project announced
events.summary: Richard Stallman announced a plan to write a free Unix-compatible operating system, GNU, and the freedoms that would attach to it. The tools from that project, paired later with the Linux kernel, made a complete free system.

events.title: Domain Name System
events.summary: Paul Mockapetris published the first DNS specifications, so names like a host and a domain could stand in for numeric addresses. The system is how people still find machines on the Internet.

events.title: Apple Lisa
events.summary: Apple shipped the Lisa, the first personal computer it sold with a mouse and a graphical desktop. It was expensive and slow, and the Macintosh carried the interface to a wider public the next year.

events.title: Apple Macintosh
events.summary: Apple introduced the Macintosh, a mouse-driven computer with a graphical interface on a Motorola 68000. A Super Bowl commercial that month framed it as a personal machine against the IBM PC.

events.title: Flash memory
events.summary: Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba presented flash memory, a non-volatile chip that could be erased in blocks and rewritten. Memory cards, USB sticks, and solid-state drives descend from it.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Memory and storage

events.title: 4.2BSD networking
events.summary: The Berkeley Software Distribution added a TCP/IP stack that many machines actually ran. BSD, not only the Bell Labs tree, is how the Internet protocols spread onto Unix systems.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web
Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.note: Berkeley's TCP/IP work was funded by DARPA and shipped in 4.2BSD in 1983. The FreeBSD project itself forked later, in 1993.

events.title: The C++ Programming Language
events.summary: Bjarne Stroustrup's book presented C++, his extension of C with classes and stronger types. The language became a standard tool for large software and for games.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.note: Stroustrup's "C with Classes" dates to 1979, and the name C++ to 1983. This entry marks the 1985 book that published the language.

events.title: Windows 1.0
events.summary: Microsoft released Windows 1.0, a graphical shell on top of MS-DOS. It did not displace DOS, but it started the Windows line.

events.title: Intel 80386
events.summary: Intel introduced the 80386, a 32-bit member of the x86 family with a mode that could still run older software. It made graphical operating systems on PCs practical.

events.title: Amiga 1000
events.summary: Commodore launched the Amiga 1000, a Motorola 68000 computer with custom chips for graphics and sound beyond most personal computers of the year. It kept a devoted following for video and games.

events.title: The WELL
events.summary: The Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link opened as a dial-up conferencing system in the Bay Area. It became a model of an online community with real names and long-running conversations.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: NSFNET
events.summary: The US National Science Foundation started NSFNET, a backbone linking academic supercomputer centers. It, more than the original ARPANET, carried the growing research Internet.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Connection Machine
events.summary: Thinking Machines introduced the CM-1, Danny Hillis's massively parallel computer aimed at symbolic and AI workloads. Thousands of simple processors shared a programmable network.

events.title: Compaq Deskpro 386
events.summary: Compaq shipped a PC compatible built on the Intel 80386 before IBM did. Clone makers, not only IBM, now set the pace of the x86 PC.

events.title: Acorn Archimedes and ARM
events.summary: Acorn shipped the Archimedes, the first computer to use its own ARM RISC processor. ARM was later spun out to license low-power designs, which came to dominate phones.

events.title: Perl
events.summary: Larry Wall released Perl, a practical language for text, reports, and system administration. It became a glue language of the early Web.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: HyperCard
events.summary: Bill Atkinson designed HyperCard for the Macintosh, a stack of linked cards that non-programmers could build. It revived hypertext on personal computers and influenced later authoring tools.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages
Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: World Wide Web proposal
events.summary: Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN, wrote a proposal for a hypertext system to share information across the laboratory's computers. The note is the start of the Web.

sources.title: W3C — A little history of the World Wide Web

events.title: Intel 80486
events.summary: Intel released the 80486, an x86 chip with an on-chip cache and, in many versions, a built-in floating-point unit. It carried PC software into the 1990s.

events.title: Windows 3.0
events.summary: Microsoft shipped Windows 3.0, the first Windows that large numbers of PC users actually ran. It still sat on DOS, but the graphical environment became the one people bought software for.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: ARM Ltd
events.summary: Acorn, Apple, and VLSI Technology formed Advanced RISC Machines to license the ARM architecture. The company sold designs rather than finished chips, which is how ARM ended up in phones.

events.title: The first website
events.summary: The first website, info.cern.ch, went live at CERN, describing the World Wide Web project itself. Berners-Lee had prototyped the server, URLs, HTML, and a browser on a NeXT machine the year before.

sources.title: W3C — A little history of the World Wide Web

events.note: Berners-Lee's chronology on the W3C site lists the project files as posted to alt.hypertext in August 1991, including the 6th.

events.title: Linux kernel announced
events.summary: Linus Torvalds posted that he was building a free Unix-like kernel for 386 PCs. Combined with GNU tools, Linux became a widely used operating system for servers, phones, and supercomputers.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Python 0.9.0
events.summary: Guido van Rossum released Python 0.9.0, a language meant to be readable, with exceptions and functions as first-class values. It later became a standard language for scripting, science, and machine learning.

events.title: Difference Engine No. 2 is built
events.summary: The Science Museum in London finished a Difference Engine No. 2 from Babbage's later drawings, using methods available in his time. The build showed that the design could have worked.

sources.title: Science Museum Group — Babbage's difference engines

events.title: NCSA Mosaic
events.summary: The National Center for Supercomputing Applications released Mosaic, a graphical browser for the Web that showed images in the page. It took the Web from a specialist tool to something a newcomer could use.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Intel Pentium
events.summary: Intel named its next x86 processor Pentium and added superscalar execution so it could work on more than one instruction at a time. The name stuck for a generation of PCs.

events.title: FreeBSD
events.summary: The FreeBSD project shipped a complete open Unix-like system descended from BSD. It became a common operating system for servers on the Internet.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Java announced
events.summary: Sun Microsystems announced Java, an object-oriented language designed so compiled programs could run on many kinds of machines. It became a standard language for servers and, for a time, for the browser.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: JavaScript
events.summary: Brendan Eich created JavaScript at Netscape so pages could respond to the reader without a round trip to the server. It became the programming language of the Web browser.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.note: A prototype was written at Netscape in May 1995. The language reached users in Netscape Navigator 2 later that year. Which day counts as the birthday is disputed.

events.title: Windows 95
events.summary: Microsoft released Windows 95, with a Start menu, a desktop, and built-in networking, as the operating system most new PCs shipped with. It moved mainstream personal computing off the DOS prompt.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Apache HTTP Server
events.summary: A group of webmasters coordinated patches to the NCSA web server and released Apache. It became the most widely used web server of the late 1990s and 2000s.

events.title: NSFNET backbone retired
events.summary: The National Science Foundation retired its NSFNET backbone and left long-haul Internet traffic to commercial networks. The public Internet was no longer a research network with a single sponsored spine.

sources.title: NSF — A brief history of NSF and the Internet
Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: 3dfx Voodoo
events.summary: 3dfx shipped the Voodoo graphics accelerator, an add-in card that drew 3D games much faster than a CPU alone. Dedicated 3D boards became part of a PC.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Graphics and games

events.title: Palm Pilot
events.summary: Palm released a pocket organizer with a stylus alphabet called Graffiti and a cradle that synchronized with a PC. It made a handheld computer an ordinary object before smartphones.

events.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
events.summary: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. The Computer History Museum records the score as two wins for the machine, one for Kasparov, and three draws.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: ASCI Red
events.summary: Intel delivered ASCI Red to Sandia National Laboratories for nuclear-stockpile simulations after underground testing ended. It led the list of the fastest supercomputers into 2000.

events.title: DOCSIS cable modems
events.summary: CableLabs published the DOCSIS specification so cable-television networks could carry data with interoperable modems. It is the standard behind consumer cable broadband.

events.title: Universal Serial Bus
events.summary: Intel and partner companies published USB so keyboards, drives, and other peripherals could share one plug-and-play connector. It replaced a clutter of PC ports.

events.title: Google
events.summary: Larry Page and Sergey Brin incorporated Google, built around ranking web pages by the links among them. Search, rather than directories, became the way most people entered the Web.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Open source
events.summary: A group of free-software developers adopted the term open source and founded the Open Source Initiative. The name described a practical way to share source code, alongside the GNU idea of software freedom.

sources.title: Open Source Initiative — History of the OSI

events.title: iMac
events.summary: Apple launched the iMac, a translucent all-in-one Macintosh, after Steve Jobs returned. It dropped older ports in favor of USB and marked Apple's recovery as a consumer-computer company.

events.title: Wi-Fi at home
events.summary: The Wi-Fi Alliance and the faster IEEE 802.11b specification put wireless local networks into homes and small offices. The original IEEE 802.11 standard had been approved in 1997.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.note: Home Wi-Fi is dated here to 1999 and 802.11b. The first IEEE 802.11 standard was approved in 1997.

events.title: NVIDIA GeForce 256
events.summary: NVIDIA introduced the GeForce 256 and marketed it as a graphics processing unit, taking transform and lighting off the CPU. Programmable GPUs later became the hardware of both games and deep learning.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Graphics and games

events.title: Mac OS X
events.summary: Apple released Mac OS X, a new Macintosh operating system built on the Unix-derived foundation acquired with NeXT. It replaced the classic Mac OS.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Wikipedia
events.summary: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched Wikipedia, a free encyclopedia anyone could edit. It became a default public reference, written by volunteers.

events.title: Windows XP
events.summary: Microsoft released Windows XP, merging the consumer Windows line with the NT kernel. It stayed the usual PC operating system for years.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: Earth Simulator
events.summary: Japan's Earth Simulator, a NEC vector machine built for climate modeling, led the rankings of the fastest supercomputers. It held that place from 2002 until 2004.

events.title: AMD Opteron and x86-64
events.summary: AMD shipped the Opteron, extending x86 to 64-bit addresses while still running existing 32-bit software. Intel later adopted a compatible 64-bit mode, and it became the ordinary PC and server architecture.

events.title: Git
events.summary: Linus Torvalds wrote Git to manage Linux kernel source after a break with the previous version-control host. Distributed version control became the normal way software is collaborated on.

sources.title: Git — A short history of Git

events.title: Amazon S3
events.summary: Amazon Web Services launched Simple Storage Service, renting disk by the request instead of selling a computer. Public cloud storage and, soon after, rented virtual machines grew from that offer.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Networking and the Web

events.title: Hadoop
events.summary: The Hadoop project packaged a MapReduce-style system for processing large data sets across ordinary servers. It became a standard tool of big-data work before cloud warehouses absorbed much of the job.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — Software and languages

events.title: One Laptop per Child
events.summary: Nicholas Negroponte announced One Laptop per Child at the World Economic Forum, aiming at a cheap connected laptop for schools in poor countries. Millions of the XO laptops were eventually shipped.

events.title: Amazon Kindle
events.summary: Amazon released the Kindle, an electronic reader with wireless access to its bookstore. E-ink reading devices moved from prototypes to a mass product.

events.title: Apple announces the iPhone
events.summary: Apple announced the iPhone, a touchscreen phone, iPod, and web browser in one device, and said it would go on sale in June. The phone's operating system, later named iOS, set the pattern for smartphones.

sources.title: Apple Newsroom — Apple reinvents the phone

events.note: Announced 9 January 2007. Apple said it would go on sale in the United States on 29 June 2007.

events.title: Android announced
events.summary: The Open Handset Alliance, led by Google, announced Android, an open software stack for mobile phones. The first phone to ship with it arrived the following year.

events.title: T-Mobile G1
events.summary: The T-Mobile G1, also called the HTC Dream, was the first phone sold with Android. It paired a touchscreen with a physical keyboard and the Android Market.

events.title: Roadrunner
events.summary: IBM's Roadrunner at Los Alamos was the first computer to sustain a petaflop, a thousand trillion floating-point operations per second. It mixed IBM Cell processors with AMD Opterons.

events.title: MacBook Air and the SSD laptop
events.summary: Apple introduced the MacBook Air, a thin laptop that, in the Computer History Museum's account, was the first mass-market computer to replace the hard drive with solid-state storage. Flash moved from cameras and sticks into the main disk of a laptop.

events.title: Raspberry Pi
events.summary: The Raspberry Pi Foundation released a cheap single-board computer to teach computing. It also became a standard board for hobbyist hardware projects.

events.title: Watson on Jeopardy!
events.summary: IBM's Watson defeated two Jeopardy! champions on television, answering clues in ordinary language. It was a public demonstration of question-answering software trained on large text collections.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: Apple iPad
events.summary: Apple announced the iPad, a tablet that ran the iPhone's operating system on a larger screen. Tablets became a mainstream computer beside the phone and the laptop.

events.title: Siri
events.summary: Apple shipped Siri with the iPhone 4S, a spoken assistant on the phone. Voice interfaces moved from a research demo to something millions of people could try.

sources.title: Computer History Museum — AI and robotics

events.title: Docker
events.summary: Solomon Hykes's Docker, shown publicly in 2013, made Linux containers easy to package and ship. It changed how server software is built and deployed.

sources.title: PyCon 2013 — The future of Linux containers

events.title: Kubernetes
events.summary: Google released Kubernetes, an open system for running containers across a cluster, drawn from its internal Borg scheduler. It became the usual control plane for cloud applications.

events.title: Rust 1.0
events.summary: The Rust project released version 1.0, a systems language that checks memory safety at compile time without a garbage collector. It has since been adopted for browsers, tools, and operating-system components.

events.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol
events.summary: DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's strongest Go players, in a five-game match in Seoul. The result marked how far deep reinforcement learning had come on a game long thought hostile to brute force.

sources.title: Nature — Mastering the game of Go

events.title: AlexNet and ImageNet
events.summary: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton's convolutional network won the 2012 ImageNet image-recognition contest by a wide margin. The result is the usual marker for the start of the deep-learning boom.

sources.title: NeurIPS — ImageNet classification with deep convolutional neural networks

events.note: The ImageNet competition result was in 2012. The conference paper appeared at NeurIPS in December 2012.

events.title: Attention Is All You Need
events.summary: Vaswani and colleagues posted the transformer architecture, which uses attention instead of recurrence to model sequences. Later large language models are built on that design.

sources.title: arXiv — Attention Is All You Need

events.title: GPT-3
events.summary: OpenAI described GPT-3, a very large language model that could perform many text tasks from a prompt without task-specific training. It showed how far scale and transformers would go before chat products made them famous.

sources.title: arXiv — Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

events.title: Apple M1
events.summary: Apple announced the M1, its own system-on-a-chip for the Mac, leaving Intel processors in that line. The chip brought the phone-class ARM designs Apple had shipped for a decade into its personal computers.

events.title: ChatGPT
events.summary: OpenAI released ChatGPT, a conversational interface on a large language model. Within weeks it made generative language tools a public habit rather than a research demo.

events.title: Frontier passes exascale
events.summary: Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Frontier system was reported as the first to pass one exaflop on the TOP500 benchmark. Exascale computing moved from a target to an installed machine.

events.title: GPT-4
events.summary: OpenAI released GPT-4, a multimodal model that accepted images as well as text and scored far higher than its predecessor on many exams and benchmarks. It became the model behind a wave of commercial assistants.

events.title: El Capitan leads the TOP500
events.summary: Lawrence Livermore's El Capitan, built by HPE with AMD processors and GPUs, led the November 2024 TOP500 list. It took the top supercomputer ranking from the previous exascale machines.

events.title: RISC-V
events.summary: Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, published RISC-V, an open instruction set anyone can implement without a license fee. Chips, boards, and teaching tools have since been built on it.
